quests.hint: Two writers sharing credit on the same novel because they wrote it together.
quests.explanation: CO- means 'together' or 'jointly.' CO- + AUTHOR = COAUTHOR, a person who writes something jointly with someone else.
quests.instruction: Which prefix fits the meaning below?

quests.hint: The pilot's partner in the cockpit, sharing control of the plane.
quests.explanation: COPILOT combines CO- with PILOT, naming a second pilot who shares flying duties with the main pilot.
quests.instruction: Which word matches this situation?

quests.hint: The person sitting at the next desk in your office, doing a related job.
quests.explanation: CO- + WORKER = COWORKER, someone who works together with you. EX- would instead mean a former worker, someone who no longer holds that role — a very different relationship.
quests.instruction: Which prefix correctly completes this word?

quests.hint: A person you were once married to, but no longer are.
quests.explanation: EX- means 'former' or 'outside of.' EX- + HUSBAND = EX-HUSBAND, a person's former husband.
quests.instruction: Which prefix fits the meaning below?

quests.hint: The team's previous coach, who left the club at the end of last season.
quests.explanation: EX-COACH is EX- + COACH, referring to someone who used to hold that position but no longer does.
quests.instruction: Which word matches this situation?

quests.hint: Someone leaving a country to remove themselves entirely from public political life.
quests.explanation: EX- can also mean 'out of' or 'away from,' as in EXIT (going out) or EXPORT (sending goods out). Here it points to leaving or existing outside a place, distinct from CO-, which brings people together.
quests.instruction: Which prefix correctly completes this word?

quests.hint: The quality that makes a joke land, or a painting look genuinely inventive.
quests.explanation: -ITY turns an adjective into a noun naming a quality or state. ORIGINAL + -ITY = ORIGINALITY, the quality of being original.
quests.meaningBreakdown: ORIGINAL (root) + ITY (suffix, forms a noun of quality)
quests.instruction: Which suffix fits the meaning below?

quests.hint: The power a public speaker has to hold an audience's attention without using notes.
quests.explanation: ABILITY is formed from ABLE + -ITY (the E drops before the suffix), naming the quality or power to do something.
quests.meaningBreakdown: ABIL (root, silent e dropped) + ITY (suffix, forms a noun of quality)
quests.instruction: Which word matches this situation?

quests.hint: The formal wording expected in a business letter, as opposed to a text to a friend.
quests.explanation: -ITY builds FORMALITY from FORMAL, the quality of being formal. -ISH would instead suggest 'somewhat formal,' a vague approximation rather than a defined quality.
quests.meaningBreakdown: FORMAL (root) + ITY (suffix, forms a noun of quality)
quests.instruction: Which suffix correctly completes this word?

quests.hint: The person a violinist studies with for years to master their craft.
quests.explanation: -IST names a person associated with a skill, belief, or practice. VIOLIN + -IST = VIOLINIST, a person who plays the violin.
quests.instruction: Which suffix fits the meaning below?

quests.hint: Someone whose entire career is spent studying rocks and the layers of the Earth.
quests.explanation: GEOLOGIST is GEOLOGY + -IST (the Y drops before the suffix), a person who specializes in the science of the Earth.
quests.instruction: Which word matches this situation?

quests.hint: Someone who creates paintings, sculptures, or other creative works professionally.
quests.explanation: -IST forms ARTIST from ART, a person devoted to a craft or field. -ER would produce a different-sounding word here, and English speakers specifically say ARTIST, not 'arter,' for this profession.
quests.instruction: Which suffix correctly completes this word?

quests.hint: A shirt that's more or less blue, but not quite an exact match to the paint sample.
quests.explanation: -ISH means 'somewhat' or 'approximately.' BLUE + -ISH = BLUISH, somewhat blue, not a precise shade.
quests.instruction: Which suffix fits the meaning below?

quests.hint: Describing a grown adult who throws a tantrum when they don't get their way.
quests.explanation: CHILDISH is built from CHILD + -ISH, describing behavior that resembles a child's — usually meant as criticism when an adult acts that way.
quests.instruction: Which word matches this situation?

quests.hint: Describing someone who only ever thinks about their own wants, never anyone else's.
quests.explanation: -ISH turns SELF into SELFISH, focused only on one's own needs. -OUS would instead usually mean 'full of' a quality (like DANGEROUS), which doesn't fit the specific 'resembling/characterized by' sense -ISH carries here.
quests.instruction: Which suffix correctly completes this word?

quests.hint: What happens to butter left out on the counter on a hot day.
quests.explanation: -EN can turn an adjective into a verb meaning 'to make' or 'to become.' SOFT + -EN = SOFTEN, to make or become soft.
quests.instruction: Which suffix fits the meaning below?

quests.hint: What a gardener does to loosen packed soil before planting seeds.
quests.explanation: LOOSEN is LOOSE + -EN, meaning to make something loose or to release tension.
quests.instruction: Which word matches this situation?

quests.hint: What a knife loses after cutting through so many vegetables that it needs a whetstone.
quests.explanation: -EN turns SHARP into SHARPEN, to make something sharp. -ISH would instead soften a description ('somewhat sharp'), not describe an action of making something so.
quests.instruction: Which suffix correctly completes this word?

quests.hint: A soup with big chunks of vegetables and beans, instead of a smooth broth.
quests.explanation: -Y turns a noun into an adjective describing something characterized by or full of that thing. CHUNK + -Y = CHUNKY, full of chunks.
quests.instruction: Which suffix fits the meaning below?

quests.hint: A beach where your feet sink into the ground with every step.
quests.explanation: SANDY is SAND + -Y, describing a surface covered in or made up of sand.
quests.instruction: Which word matches this situation?

quests.hint: A sky completely covered from horizon to horizon, blocking out the sun.
quests.explanation: -Y forms CLOUDY from CLOUD, full of clouds. -OUS would technically attach to some nouns to mean 'full of' too, but CLOUD specifically pairs with -Y, not -OUS, in standard English.
quests.instruction: Which suffix correctly completes this word?

quests.hint: A cliffside hike where one careless step could send you tumbling down.
quests.explanation: -OUS means 'full of' or 'having the quality of.' DANGER + -OUS = DANGEROUS, full of danger.
quests.instruction: Which suffix fits the meaning below?

quests.hint: A billionaire's mansion, complete with a private movie theater and indoor pool.
quests.explanation: LUXURIOUS is LUXURY + -OUS (with a spelling shift), describing something full of luxury and comfort.
quests.instruction: Which word matches this situation?

quests.hint: Describing a singer so widely known that strangers recognize her on the street.
quests.explanation: -OUS builds FAMOUS from FAME (with the silent E dropped), full of fame. -Y wouldn't work here — 'famy' isn't an English word, showing that not every noun accepts every adjective-forming suffix.
quests.meaningBreakdown: FAM (root, silent e dropped) + OUS (suffix, 'full of')
quests.instruction: Which suffix correctly completes this word?

quests.hint: A checkup you schedule with a doctor once a year, not because you're sick.
quests.explanation: -AL turns a noun into an adjective meaning 'relating to.' ANNUAL comes from ANNU- ('year') + -AL, meaning happening once a year.
quests.instruction: Which suffix fits the meaning below?

quests.hint: A problem with your bank account balance, not with your health or your car.
quests.explanation: FINANCIAL is FINANCE + -AL (with a spelling shift), meaning relating to money matters.
quests.instruction: Which word matches this situation?

quests.hint: A holiday celebrated by every state and every citizen of a country, not just one town.
quests.explanation: -AL forms NATIONAL from NATION, relating to an entire country. -OUS would instead suggest 'full of a quality' rather than 'relating to,' which doesn't fit how we describe something as belonging to a nation.
quests.instruction: Which suffix correctly completes this word?

quests.hint: Think back over this unit: which suffix builds an adjective meaning 'relating to' a noun, rather than 'full of' one?
quests.explanation: -AL means 'relating to' (NATIONAL, FINANCIAL), while -OUS means 'full of' (DANGEROUS, FAMOUS) and -Y often means 'covered in' (SANDY, CLOUDY). Three suffixes, three related but distinct jobs.
quests.instruction: Review: which suffix means 'relating to,' not 'full of' or 'covered in'?

quests.hint: A teacher's former student who now runs a successful company across town.
quests.explanation: EX-STUDENT combines EX- ('former') with STUDENT, someone who used to study there but has since moved on — a useful review of EX- alongside this unit's new -AL and -OUS words.
quests.instruction: Which word matches this situation?

quests.hint: Describing a chemistry teacher who specializes in and has deep training in the subject.
quests.explanation: -IST forms CHEMIST from CHEMISTRY (with the -ISTRY shortened to the root), a person devoted to that field of science — closing out the unit's review of person-naming and quality-naming suffixes together.
quests.instruction: Review: which suffix correctly completes this word?
